cards.front: Define the span of a set of vectors $S = \{\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k\}$.
cards.back:
The span of a set of vectors $S$, denoted as $\text{span}(S)$ or $\text{span}(\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k)$, is the set of all possible linear combinations of those vectors.
Mathematically, $\text{span}(S) = \{c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2\mathbf{v}_2 + \ldots + c_k\mathbf{v}_k \mid c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_k \in \mathbb{R}\}$.

cards.front: Define a linear combination of vectors $\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k$.
cards.back: A linear combination of vectors $\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k$ is an expression of the form $c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2\mathbf{v}_2 + \ldots + c_k\mathbf{v}_k$, where $c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_k$ are scalars (usually real numbers).

cards.front: Geometrically, what does $\text{span}(\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2)$ represent if $\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2 \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and are not parallel?
cards.back: The span of two non-parallel vectors $\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ represents the unique plane passing through the origin that contains both vectors. Any point on this plane can be reached by scaling and adding $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$.

To check if $\mathbf{w} \in \text{span}(\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k)$, you must determine if $\mathbf{w}$ can be written as a linear combination of $\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k$. This means finding scalars $c_1, \ldots, c_k$ such that:
$$c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2\mathbf{v}_2 + \ldots + c_k\mathbf{v}_k = \mathbf{w}$$
This equation can be rewritten as a system of linear equations (often in matrix form $A\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{w}$, where $A$ has columns $\mathbf{v}_i$). If the system is consistent (has at least one solution), then $\mathbf{w}$ is in the span.

cards.front: Prove that $\mathbf{0} \in \text{span}(\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k)$ for any non-empty set of vectors.
cards.back:
By definition, the span of a set of vectors is the set of all possible linear combinations. We can form a linear combination where all scalars are zero:
$$0\mathbf{v}_1 + 0\mathbf{v}_2 + \ldots + 0\mathbf{v}_k = \mathbf{0}$$
Since the zero vector can be expressed as a linear combination of the vectors in $S$, it is by definition an element of $\text{span}(S)$.

cards.front: Describe $\text{span}(\mathbf{v})$ for a single non-zero vector $\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n$.
cards.back:
The span of a single non-zero vector $\mathbf{v}$ is the set of all scalar multiples of $\mathbf{v}$. Geometrically, this represents a line passing through the origin in the direction of $\mathbf{v}$.
Mathematically, $\text{span}(\mathbf{v}) = \{c\mathbf{v} \mid c \in \mathbb{R}\}$.

cards.front: Explain why $\text{span}(S)$ is always a subspace of the vector space it belongs to.
cards.back:
A set $W$ is a subspace if it satisfies three conditions:
1.  **Contains the zero vector:** As shown previously, $\mathbf{0} \in \text{span}(S)$ by taking all scalars to be zero.
2.  **Closed under vector addition:** If $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{w} \in \text{span}(S)$, then $\mathbf{u} = \sum c_i\mathbf{v}_i$ and $\mathbf{w} = \sum d_i\mathbf{v}_i$. Their sum is $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w} = \sum (c_i+d_i)\mathbf{v}_i$, which is also a linear combination of vectors in $S$, so $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w} \in \text{span}(S)$.
3.  **Closed under scalar multiplication:** If $\mathbf{u} \in \text{span}(S)$ and $k$ is a scalar, then $\mathbf{u} = \sum c_i\mathbf{v}_i$. Then $k\mathbf{u} = k(\sum c_i\mathbf{v}_i) = \sum (kc_i)\mathbf{v}_i$, which is also a linear combination of vectors in $S$, so $k\mathbf{u} \in \text{span}(S)$.
Since all three conditions are met, $\text{span}(S)$ is a subspace.
